items.q: No sooner (A) the bell had rung than the entire class (B) poured into the corridor, (C) leaving their unfinished worksheets (D) scattered across the desks.
items.explanation: After the negative adverbial No sooner the auxiliary must be inverted with the subject: No sooner had the bell rung than …

items.q: The head coach (A) insisted that every player (B) arrives at the stadium an hour early (C) so that the physiotherapist could (D) check on any lingering injuries.
items.explanation: A demand reported with insist that takes the bare subjunctive: insisted that every player arrive, with no -s regardless of tense.

items.q: Although the expedition (A) had been planned for months, the climbers (B) found that they had brought (C) too few equipment (D) to survive a second night on the ridge.
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable, so it takes little / less, not few / fewer: too little equipment.

items.q: Only when the last guest (A) had left (B) did my mother admit (C) how nervous she had been about (D) to host the dinner.
options: how nervous she had been about
items.explanation: A verb after the preposition about must be a gerund: nervous about hosting, never about to host in this sense.

items.q: If only I (A) listened to my grandfather's advice about saving money, I (B) would not be struggling (C) to pay for the school trip (D) that everyone else is joining.
options: to pay for the school trip
items.explanation: If only / wish about a past regret takes the past perfect: If only I had listened; the present result (would not be struggling) makes this a mixed conditional.

items.q: (A) Walking along the harbour at dawn, (B) the fishing boats seemed to glide (C) silently past us, (D) their lanterns still glowing in the mist.
options: Walking along the harbour at dawn
the fishing boats seemed to glide
their lanterns still glowing in the mist
items.correction: we watched the fishing boats glide
items.explanation: A dangling participle: the clause Walking along the harbour must describe the subject of the main clause, and boats cannot walk, so the subject has to be we.

items.q: The new fitness app (A) lets users track their sleep, (B) count their steps and (C) to log every meal (D) without typing a word.
items.explanation: Parallelism: the three verbs after lets users must share one form (bare infinitive): track, count and log.

items.q: The trekkers (A) were warned that the weather (B) could change without notice and that they (C) should keep a close (D) look on the sky.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is keep a close eye on something; look does not combine with keep … on.

items.q: It was (A) so a gripping novel that (B) my sister finished it in one sitting, (C) ignoring her mother's repeated calls (D) to come down for dinner.
options: my sister finished it in one sitting
items.explanation: Before a + adjective + noun we use such: such a gripping novel that; so stands directly before an adjective (so gripping a novel).

items.q: If the engineers (A) had inspected the dam more carefully last spring, the village (B) would not have been flooded now and (C) hundreds of families (D) would still have their homes.
options: would not have been flooded now
items.explanation: A mixed conditional: a past condition (had inspected) with a present result marked by now takes would + bare infinitive, not would have.

items.q: The guide told us that the temple (A) had been built in the ninth century and that (B) we should remove our shoes (C) before we will enter (D) the inner courtyard.
items.explanation: A time clause after before never takes will, and reported speech backshifts anyway: before entering or before we entered.

items.q: The government (A) promised generous help after the earthquake, (B) yet six months later (C) the villagers had seen (D) far fewer progress than they had been promised.
items.explanation: Progress is uncountable, so the comparative quantifier is less: far less progress, never fewer.

items.q: (A) Although the recipe's insistence on fresh basil, my aunt (B) substituted dried herbs and the dish (C) still tasted (D) far better than we had expected.
options: far better than we had expected
items.explanation: Although introduces a clause with a verb; before a noun phrase (the recipe's insistence) we need despite / in spite of.

items.q: The committee (A) reached the conclusion that the museum (B) should make further research into the painting's origin before (C) putting it on display (D) to the public.
items.explanation: Research collocates with do / carry out / conduct, not make: carry out further research into.

items.q: (A) Whether the bridge (B) will be finished on time (C) depends largely on weather, which (D) has been unusually wet this year.
options: has been unusually wet this year
items.explanation: Weather meaning the specific conditions of a place or time takes the definite article: depends on the weather; the relative clause which has been unusually wet this year shows it is this year’s particular weather, not weather in general.

items.q: The queue for the new roller coaster (A) moved so slowly that (B) my little brother, (C) who had begged to come, (D) refused to endure a such long wait.
options: refused to endure a such long wait
items.correction: refused to endure such a long wait
items.explanation: Such comes before the article: such a long wait; only so allows the pattern so long a wait.

items.q: Not only (A) the storm damaged the greenhouse, (B) but it also (C) uprooted the apple trees (D) my grandfather had planted decades earlier.
options: my grandfather had planted decades earlier
items.correction: did the storm damage the greenhouse
items.explanation: When Not only opens the sentence, the first clause is inverted with an auxiliary: Not only did the storm damage … but it also …

items.q: What (A) impresses me most about the documentary (B) are the way (C) it lets the villagers (D) speak for themselves.
items.explanation: In a what-cleft the subject What impresses me most is singular, so the linking verb is is: What … is the way …

items.q: If the ancient library (A) had not burned down, scholars today (B) would probably (C) had access to texts (D) that survive only as fragments.
items.explanation: A past condition with a present result (scholars today) is a mixed conditional: would + bare infinitive, so would have access, not would had.

items.q: The lighthouse, (A) whose lamp (B) has guided ships for a century, (C) now belongs to a trust (D) which members maintain it on weekends.
options: has guided ships for a century
which members maintain it on weekends
items.correction: whose members maintain it on weekends
items.explanation: Possession inside a relative clause (the members of the trust) is expressed with whose: a trust whose members …

items.q: (A) Exhausting by the twelve-hour flight, the delegates (B) barely managed to stay awake (C) during the welcome speech (D) delivered by the mayor.
items.explanation: A participle clause describing how the subject felt uses the past participle: Exhausted by; -ing would mean the delegates were causing exhaustion.

items.q: (A) Scarcely had the ferry left the harbour (B) as a thick fog rolled in, (C) forcing the captain (D) to cut the engines and wait.
options: Scarcely had the ferry left the harbour
as a thick fog rolled in
to cut the engines and wait
items.correction: when a thick fog rolled in
items.explanation: Scarcely / hardly pairs with when (and no sooner with than): Scarcely had … when …

items.q: The old fisherman (A) often says he (B) wishes he (C) can go back to the days (D) when the river was full of carp.
options: can go back to the days
when the river was full of carp
items.correction: could go back to the days
items.explanation: After wish an unreal present or impossible desire takes a past form: wishes he could go back, not can.

items.q: Among the items (A) recovered from the shipwreck (B) were a bronze compass, a set of silver spoons and a leather-bound journal (C) whose pages (D) was still legible.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the plural head pages, not with journal: whose pages were still legible.

items.q: The scientist (A) whom discovered the bacterium (B) refused to name it after herself, (C) preferring a Latin word (D) meaning 'stubborn'.
options: refused to name it after herself
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of discovered, so it must be who; whom is only for the object of a verb or preposition.

items.q: The northern provinces (A) receive most of their rain in summer, (B) however the south (C) stays dry until (D) well into October.
options: receive most of their rain in summer
items.explanation: However is an adverb and cannot join two clauses with a comma; a contrast between clauses needs the conjunction whereas / while.

items.q: The scholarship rewards students (A) who not only (B) excel academically but also (C) contributing to their communities (D) through voluntary work.
items.explanation: Not only … but also must join parallel forms: excel and contribute, both finite verbs in the relative clause.

items.q: The more carefully you (A) proofread your essay, (B) the fewer mistakes (C) the examiner will find, and (D) the highest your mark will be.
options: the highest your mark will be
items.correction: the higher your mark will be
items.explanation: The pattern the more … the more uses comparatives throughout: the higher your mark will be, not a superlative.

items.q: Between you and (A) I, the referee's decision (B) had far more to do with the crowd (C) than with anything (D) that happened on the pitch.
options: had far more to do with the crowd
items.explanation: A pronoun after the preposition between is an object pronoun: between you and me.

items.q: The residents (A) have demanded that the council (B) will repair the flooded underpass (C) before the monsoon season (D) begins in earnest.
items.explanation: Demand that is followed by the subjunctive (bare infinitive): demanded that the council repair; will is not used in this clause.

items.q: The nutritionist (A) suggested that the school canteen (B) replace sugary drinks with water and (C) offers fruit (D) at every meal.
items.explanation: Both verbs after suggested that stay in the subjunctive: replace … and offer; the second verb cannot switch to offers.

items.q: The trainee pilot (A) apologised (B) for the bumpy landing, (C) blaming a sudden gust (D) that she had been unprepared to.
options: that she had been unprepared to
items.correction: that she had been unprepared for
items.explanation: Unprepared takes the preposition for, and in a relative clause it is stranded at the end: a gust that she had been unprepared for.

items.q: The documentary (A) is concerned about the ways (B) in which coral reefs (C) recover from bleaching (D) when water temperatures fall.
items.explanation: Concerned with means about / dealing with a subject; concerned about means worried, which a documentary cannot be.

items.q: Of the two proposals, the second (A) is by far the (B) most practical, (C) though it would cost the club (D) nearly twice as much.
options: though it would cost the club
items.explanation: Comparing two things takes the comparative, even with the: the more practical of the two; the superlative needs three or more.

items.q: The planning board (A) rejected the plan (B) to widen the road, (C) being too expensive and (D) likely to increase traffic.
items.correction: as it was too expensive and
items.explanation: A dangling participle: being too expensive attaches to the subject of the main clause, the planning board, yet it is the plan that is expensive, so the reason needs its own clause: as it was too expensive and likely to …

items.q: My aunt (A) has lived abroad for a decade, (B) yet she still speaks (C) the dialect of her home town as fluently as (D) she did before she has left.
options: has lived abroad for a decade
the dialect of her home town as fluently as
she did before she has left
items.explanation: A finished past event at a definite point (before she left) takes the past simple; the present perfect cannot sit inside a past time clause.

items.q: (A) Hardly the orchestra had finished tuning up (B) when the lights failed, (C) plunging the concert hall (D) into total darkness.
options: Hardly the orchestra had finished tuning up
items.correction: Hardly had the orchestra finished tuning up
items.explanation: A sentence beginning with Hardly requires subject–auxiliary inversion: Hardly had the orchestra finished … when …

items.q: It was the referee's decision, (A) not the players' effort, (B) what cost the team (C) the championship (D) they had chased for years.
items.explanation: An it-cleft (It was X …) continues with that (or who), never what: It was the referee's decision that cost …

items.q: The swimmers (A) completed the crossing (B) in under six hours (C) although the freezing water and (D) strong currents near the shore.
items.explanation: Although must be followed by a clause; before noun phrases (the freezing water and strong currents) use despite / in spite of.

items.q: My grandmother (A) insists on writing letters by hand, (B) whereas my grandfather (C) would happily text (D) if only he can find his glasses.
options: insists on writing letters by hand
if only he can find his glasses
items.correction: if only he could find his glasses
items.explanation: A hypothetical result with would needs a past-form condition: would text if only he could find; can belongs to a real (first) conditional.
